newsitem.title: USA: GM to add 300 jobs at Oklahoma plant.
newsitem.headline: GM to add 300 jobs at Oklahoma plant.

text.p: General Motors Corp. agreed to add more than 300 new jobs at its Oklahoma City car plant to settle a seven-week strike dominated by staffing issues, the United Auto Workers union said Wednesday.

Analysts said the promised new jobs, disclosed in documents distributed to UAW Local 1999 members, indicate GM will probably have to hire new workers to settle other labour disputes, threatening its efficiency gains.
About 3,500 workers at the plant resumed production of Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass sedans Tuesday, following a tentative agreement between GM and the UAW on Saturday night.

As part of the deal, GM also agreed to bring some work back into the plant that had been shifted to outside suppliers, including sequencing of certain parts and assembly of minor parts, such as application of the Chevrolet emblem onto the Malibu radiator grille.

The union said 150 of the new jobs were to provide relief for "overloaded" jobs, 100 were to provide vacation replacements, 30 were for new apprenticeships and 45 for the work being brought back in-house.

"I think it shows some compromise on both sides," Michael Robinet of CSM Forecasting Inc. said of the agreement. "I'm disturbed by the fact that GM is in-sourcing some work. I hope that GM is not giving up some of the major efficiency gains that it got when it put a new product in Oklahoma City."
Under the UAW national agreement with GM, the new workers will be hired at 70 percent of the full wage rate and will not reach parity for three years.
A GM spokesman declined to comment on the agreement, which is scheduled for a ratification vote Friday and Saturday.

When GM started production of the Cutlass and Malibu last year, it eliminated about 900 temporary workers at the plant, reducing the work force because the new cars were easier to build than the cars they replaced.

But, according to some union officials, the UAW had demanded GM hire as many as 500 new employees to ease an increasing workload. The strike seriously curtailed the launch of the Malibu and Cutlass, two cornerstones of GM's plan to regain market share in the important midsize car market.
GM is facing similar staffing issues at a number of other plants, including its Pontiac, Mich., truck plant, where a strike is now in its sixth week.
Negotiations continued at Pontiac with little change in position by either side.

"They're still over there in the plant, but there's not much happening," said Jim Abare, a sourcing coordinator for UAW Local 594. "General Motors has to realise we're seriously determined to end this unjust treatment of their employees."

Other plants where workers have have demanded more jobs include one in Fairfax, Kan., that builds the popular Pontiac Grand Prix and Oldsmobile Intrigue cars; a transmission plant in Warren, Mich.; a fuel-injector plant in Rochester N.Y.; and a catalytic converter plant in Oak Creek, Wis.
Strikes at the parts plants still negotiating for new local labour agreements could cause significant shutdowns of GM assembly plants in North America.
